ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was granted by the ethical committee of the Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences at Ghent University with reference number 2025-091A.
Participants were native English speakers, recruited via Prolific Academic.
Based on the given premises and reversal statement, participants had to select all buttons with true or false statements from 2-to-4 buttons.

Trials differed based on whether participants had to indicate true or false statements, the number of buttons (2, 3, 4), and the number of true (none true, one true, two true) vs. false (none false, one false, two false, three false) statements.
If participants had not clicked the submit button before the response deadline of 80 seconds, no response was registered, and the next trial started immediately.
There was no response deadline, but participants were instructed to react as fast and accurately as possible.
At the start of the study, participants provided informed consent and demographic information, including age and gender ("male," "female," "non-binary," "not listed," or "prefer not to say").
After the DR task, participants completed the VPT task and Faux Pas Recognition Test, for which the order was randomized across participants.
After both tasks, participants completed the ICAR Sample Test and the AQ-Short.
Finally, participants were debriefed and informed that they could contact the researcher via Prolific if they had any questions or would like to receive a summary of the results.
Participants were also given the option to leave a comment before finishing the study.
Eight participants were excluded because they failed more than one out of the four attention checks during the experiment.

Four additional participants were excluded because they had more than 20% trials with RTs ≤ 5 seconds during the DR task (1 participant) or because their average accuracy in the VPT task was ≤ 57% (3 participants).
Participants had an average score of 60.47% (SD = 24.39%) on the DR task.
Participants were faster (Mraw RT difference = 358 ms, SD = 527 ms) and more accurate (Mdifference = 6.75%, SD = 9.59%) on congruent compared to incongruent trials.
Participants had an average accuracy of 55.26% (SD = 19.69%) on the ICAR Sample Test.

In our previous research using Prolific samples, up to 11% of participants also scored above the 50-item AQ cut-off (Nevejans et al., 2026; Experiment 1), suggesting a possible selection bias toward individuals with elevated autism traits on Prolific, at least for this type of research.

For both power analyses, we simulated data based on two previous studies (Huang et al., 2026; Nevejans et al., 2026) and a pilot study on the Faux Pas Recognition Test. table.title: The relationship between deictic relating and perspective-taking and Theory of Mind
table.data_collection_started: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
BACKGROUND
Relational Frame Theory (RFT; Hayes et al., 2001) proposes that deictic relating provides the core behavioral unit involved in perspective-taking and Theory of Mind (ToM, Hayes et al., 2001; Hempkin et al., 2024). In this experiment, we will test the relationship between deictic relating and a complex visual perspective-taking (VPT) task and a ToM task, the faux-pas recognition test. To do so, we will use a newly developed deictic relating task, created in a previous study, a complex VPT task (Huang et al., under review), and a multiple-choice version of the faux-pas recognition test (Stone et al., 1998; Burghardt et al., 2025). The order of the complex VPT task and faux-pas recognition test will be randomized across participants. Participants will further complete the shortened International Cognitive Ability Resource (ICAR) and the 28-item version of the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-Short; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Hoekstra et al., 2010) as a measure of cognitive abilities and autism traits, respectively. 

Task details:

The Deictic Relating Task. In each trial in the deictic relating task, participants read two scenarios (e.g., “I am petting a dog in the kitchen right now. You were sleeping on the sofa yesterday”) together with an additional prompt about a perspective reversal (“If I were you and you were me”), a temporal reversal (e.g., “if now were yesterday and yesterday were now”), a spatial reversal (e.g., “if the kitchen were the sofa and the sofa were the kitchen”), or a combination of two reversals. They must select true/false statements from 2 to 4 buttons with extra statements. The task will include 24 trials, of which 12 trials will describe emotions (e.g., “I am feeling lonely at a bar right now.”) and 12 trials will describe actions. 

The Complex VPT task. The VPT task (Huang et al., under review) will contain four blocks of 48 trials in which participants observe an avatar standing at a round table with two colored balls on top. In each trial, they must indicate whether the red ball is on the left or right side from the avatar’s perspective. This perspective can be identical to the participant’s perspective (congruent trial) or the opposite (incongruent), with six different orientations around the table (congruent angles: 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°; incongruent angles: 112.5°, 135°, or 157.5°). In addition, the balls are positioned either close to or far from the avatar, and the avatar can stand on the left or right side of the screen.

The Faux-Pas Recognition Test. The task is closely based on the German multiple-choice faux-pas recognition test developed by Burghardt et al. (2025; preprint: https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/sxkac_v2). We translated the German task materials into English, changed the stories and questions back to the original materials from Stone et al. (1998), and made adjustments to some items for clarity. In this task, participants read 20 short stories (taken from Stone et al., 1998): 10 stories with a faux pas and 10 without a faux pas. After reading the story, participants first answer a yes-no question (Q1): “In the story, did anyone say something they shouldn't have said or something awkward?” 
If they indicate “yes” to this question, they must answer three additional questions: (Q2) Who said something they shouldn't have said or something awkward? (Q3) Why do you think he/she said it? (Q4) How do you think […] felt? If they answer no to Q1, questions 2, 3, and 4 are skipped for that story. For each story, participants further complete two comprehension questions. Questions 2, 3, and 4 always have four response options. Comprehension questions can have between 2 and 4 response options. The written story remains on the screen for all questions.

ICAR sample test. Finally, participants will also complete the shortened International Cognitive Ability Resource (ICAR) test (see https://icar-project.com/), including 16 items: four items from verbal reasoning (items 4, 16, 17, and 19), four items from Letter and Number series (7, 33, 34, 58), four items from Matrix Reasoning (45, 46, 47, 55), and four items from the Three-Dimensional Rotation (3,4, 6, 8) (see Condon and Revelle, 2014). 


HYPOTHESES

Primary Confirmatory Hypothesis
H1: We expect to find a negative correlation between accuracy scores on the deictic relating task and the relative reaction time (RT) congruency effect in the VPT task. 
H2: We expect to find a positive correlation between accuracy scores on the deictic relating task and performance scores (i.e., the total intention-empathy score; see below) on the faux-pas recognition test. 

Secondary Research Questions 
S1. We will test the relationship between the participants’ AQ-Short scores and their accuracy on the deictic relating task. Based on RFT, we would expect participants with higher AQ-Short scores to have lower accuracy on the deictic relating task.
S2. We will test the relationship between the participants’ AQ-Short scores and their relative RT congruency effect in the VPT task. We will check whether higher AQ-Short scores are related to a stronger relative RT congruency effect, which would indicate more difficulty with switching (visual) perspectives. 
S3. We will test the relationship between the participants’ AQ-Short scores and their performance on the faux-pas recognition test. Based on previous ToM research, we expect participants with higher AQ-Short scores to have lower performance on the faux-pas recognition test.
table.design_dependent_variables:
1.	(Accuracy) scores on the deictic relating task
The accuracy will be calculated by taking the average accuracy across all 24 trials. A trial will be coded as correct if all correct statements (i.e., either all false or all true statements, depending on the instructions) are selected and all incorrect statements are unselected. The trial will be coded as incorrect if participants make one or more mistakes or do not press the submit button before the trial deadline. 

2.	The 'relative' congruency effect on the reaction times during the complex VPT task
The congruency effect relative to average RT (referred to as the 'relative congruency effect') will be the main outcome measure for the VPT task. For each participant, the relative congruency effect is calculated by subtracting the mean RT on congruent (correct) trials from the mean RT on incongruent (correct) trials, and dividing this difference by the sum of the mean RTs for congruent and incongruent trials divided by two (i.e., (RTincon − RTcon) / ((RTincon + RTcon)/2)).

3.	Summed intention-empathy scores on the faux-pas recognition test
We based our score calculation on the study by Burghardt et al. (2025, preprint), who recommend only including the empathy score and the intention score suggested by Stone et al. (1998). 
The score calculation is the following: First, for each participant, stories are excluded if the participant answered at least one of both comprehension questions incorrectly.
Second, for each story, a score for the intention and empathy question is calculated. The scoring depends on whether the story is a faux-pas or control story, and on whether the participant answered Q1 (“In the story, did anyone say something they shouldn't have said or something awkward?”) correctly. For faux-pas stories, “yes” is the correct answer for Q1; for control stories, “no” is correct. Participants only see Q2, Q3, and Q4 if they answer “yes” to Q1.

Score on the intention question:
(1)	The participant is correct on Q1: For faux-pas stories, participants receive a point if they answer Q3 (“Why do you think he/she said it?”) correctly. For control stories, participants always receive a point, even though the question is not shown (i.e., they receive a point for not answering the question). 
(2)	The participant is incorrect on Q1: The participant receives a zero score for the intention question of the story.

Score on the empathy question: 
(1)	The participant is correct on Q1: For faux-pas stories, participants receive a point if they answer Q4 (“How do you think […] felt?”) correctly. For control stories, participants always receive a point, even though the question is not shown. 
(2)	The participant is incorrect on Q1: For faux-pas stories, participants receive a zero score (they do not receive the question). For control stories, participants still receive a point if they answer Q4 correctly. 

Third, for each participant, the sum of the scores across the intention/empathy questions (for the included stories) is taken to calculate the participant’s intention/empathy score. Burghardt et al. (2025) recommend not dividing the total scores by the number of correctly answered comprehension questions. However, because we aim to assess accuracy on the empathy and intention questions, independent of comprehension, we will take the mean score across all intention questions / empathy questions of the included stories (i.e., stories with correct comprehension questions), providing a mean intention and empathy score for each participant. 

For the current study, we will use the sum of the intention and empathy scores as the faux-pas outcome measure (ranges between 0 and 2). 


Secondary outcome measures 

4.	Total AQ-Short score 
In line with previous research (e.g., Goris et al., 2020), we will use dimensional scoring of the AQ-Short, in which item scores range from 1 to 4, as these capture more variability. In the typical binary scoring of the AQ, the categories “agree” and “definitely agree” are taken together as a score “1” and “disagree” and “definitely disagree” are taken together as a score “0”.
table.statistical_tests:
Primary Confirmatory Hypothesis 
H1: We will compute the Spearman correlation between participants’ accuracy scores on the deictic relating task and the relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task. 
H2: We will compute the Spearman correlation between participants’ accuracy scores on the deictic relating task and the summed intention-empathy score on the multiple-choice faux-pas recognition test. 
For both correlations, we will compute Bayes factors (BF) using Jeffrey’s default BF hypothesis test (Ly et al., 2016), available in the BayesFactor package in R (Morey et al., 2024).

Secondary Analysis: The relationship with autism traits 
We will compute Spearman correlations between the participants’ AQ-Short scores and
(S1) their accuracy on the deictic relating task.
(S2) their relative RT congruency effect on the complex VPT task.
(S3) their summed intention-empathy score on the multiple-choice faux-pas recognition test.
table.outliers_and_exclusions:
Inclusion criteria.

Participants are between the ages of 18-40, have completed at least 100 studies on Prolific, have a 99% (or higher) approval rating for previous studies on Prolific, did not participate in previous studies on a similar topic from our research group, and are native English speakers.

Exclusion criteria. 

Participant Exclusions. Participants will be excluded from all analyses if they have incomplete data (<80% completed on one or more tasks) for the deictic relating task, the faux-pas recognition test, or the visual perspective-taking task, or if they fail more than one of the attention checks during the experiment (in the deictic relating task and/or the AQ-Short). 
Based on the deictic relating task, participants will also be excluded from all analyses if more than 20% of their trials have RTs ≤ 5 seconds during the deictic task, as this indicates low effort responding. However, due to resource limits, if >7% of the sample is excluded based on this criterion, the criterion will be dropped, and we will instead check whether results differ based on the inclusion/exclusion of these participants.

Based on the VPT task, participants will be excluded from all analyses if their mean accuracy in the VPT task is equal to or below 57%. This cutoff (110/192) corresponds to the 97.5th percentile of a binomial distribution with 192 trials (the number of trials in the task) and a success probability of 0.5, obtained using the qbinom function in R. A two-sided 95% confidence interval would also include the 2.5th percentile. However, because our primary RT analysis is performed on trials with correct responses, we will use a one-sided exclusion threshold and exclude participants with accuracy ≤ 57%. 
Participants will be excluded from all analyses with AQ-Short scores if they have incomplete data for the AQ-Short. 

Trial Exclusions. In the faux-pas recognition test, stories are excluded if the participants responded incorrectly to one (or both) comprehension questions for the story. 
In the complex VPT task, trials will be excluded from all analyses if the log-transformed RT ≥ 3 SD below or above the participant’s mean log-transformed RT. RTs will be log-transformed to approximate a normal distribution. For the calculation of the relative RT congruency effect, incorrect trials will be excluded.
table.sample_size:
We conducted a simulation-based power analysis for the main analysis (H1), which tests the correlation between accuracies on the deictic relating task and the relative RT congruency effect in the VPT task. For the power analysis, we simulated data based on two previous experiments. The power analysis indicated that a sample size of N = 164 would allow us to detect a small correlation of r = -.25 with 90.26% power, using a significance threshold of 0.05.
We also conducted a simulation-based power analysis for the main analysis (H2), which tests the correlation between accuracy on the deictic relating task and the accuracy on the Faux-Pas recognition test. For the power analysis, we simulated data based on deictic relating scores from a previous experiment and faux-pas scores from a pilot study. The power analysis indicated that a sample size N = 164 would allow us to detect a small correlation of r = .25 with 90.05% power, using a significance threshold of 0.05.
We will collect data from 164 participants. Once 164 complete submissions have been collected, data will be screened for exclusion criteria, and excluded submissions will be replaced through additional recruitment. This process will be repeated until we obtain the preregistered minimum required sample size from the power analysis (N = 164).
table.additional_comments:
Secondary Analyses

(A)	Secondary analysis: Is the correlation between deictic relating and VPT stronger than the correlation between deictic relating and faux-pas detection? 
Recent work suggests that ToM might involve more than responding in accordance with basic deictic frames (Hempkin et al., 2024; Kavanagh et al., 2020). Moreover, Barnes-Holmes et al. (2004) already suggested that “the relational skills required to complete the perspective-taking tasks in the RFT protocols may be heavily involved specifically in Levels 1-3 of the traditional ToM tasks”. Hence, deictic relating performance might be more closely related to VPT (low-level ToM) compared to the faux-pas recognition test (high-level ToM). To explore this, we will test whether the correlation between the accuracy on deictic relating and the relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task significantly differs from the correlation between the accuracy on deictic relating and the summed intention-empathy score on the faux-pas recognition test. Based on the predictions from RFT theorists, we would expect a stronger correlation with the relative RT congruency effect. We will test the difference between these correlations using the Cocor package in R. However, we did not power for this analysis specifically. A simulation-based power analysis indicated we have 88.22% power to detect a difference of .30 between the (absolute) correlations for N = 164, if we use a significance threshold of .05 and keep the correlation of relative RT congruency effect fixed at r = -.50. 

(B)	Secondary analysis: Do AQ-Short scores correlate negatively with the faux-pas detection, intention, and empathy scores? 
Using the Stone et al. (1998) scoring, we can calculate a faux-pas detection score (Q1, Q2), an intention score (Q3), and an empathy score (Q4). To check whether certain scores on the faux-pas recognition test are more strongly related to autism traits, we will look at the correlations between the different scores and AQ-Short scores separately. We expect a negative correlation with AQ-Short scores for all faux-pas scores. The calculations for the faux-pas intention and empathy score are described above. For the faux-pas detection score, stories with one or two incorrect comprehension questions are again excluded. For faux-pas stories, (correct) answers to the first and second questions are summed (i.e., a maximum of 2 points per story). Note that, if the first question is answered incorrectly, the second question is not shown and receives a zero score as well. For control stories, if the participant answered the first question correctly, they receive 2 points. If not, they receive zero points. The Stone et al. (1998) faux-pas detection score is the sum of all scores, divided by the number of included stories (i.e., the mean score for each participant). 

(C)	Additional measure: ICAR scores
We will also collect data on the ICAR sample test as a proxy of IQ, as ToM and relational abilities might be related to intelligence as well. We will compute Spearman correlations between ICAR scores and performance on the other three measures (the relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task, the summed intention-empathy score on the faux-pas recognition test, and accuracy on the deictic relating task). The ICAR sample test has a maximum score of 16.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 213 columns across 9 data files.
#### Issues Identified
3 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("pilot study/raw/raw.csv", "preprocessed_deictic_relating_task.csv", "processed_pilot.csv"), Column = c("gender_text", "trial_num", "gender_text"), Issues = c("⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 9639 values are missing", "#️⃣ Numeric as text — Column is 92% numeric but 1 value cannot be parsed: \"XX\"", "⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 99 values are missing" )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding

6 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **6 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Respondent = c("42", "77", "90", "1", "25", "69"
), "Blocks flagged" = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L), Scales = c("aq (1-4, 6 items)",

"same answer 5 times in a row, out of 6 items (flagged at 5)", 
"same answer 5 times in a row, out of 6 items (flagged at 5)"
), "Short-scale only" = c("yes", "yes", "yes", "yes", "yes", 
"yes")), row.names = c(3L, 5L, 6L, 1L, 2L, 4L), class = "data.frame")

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 9 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

summary_table.ethics_statements: Ethical approval was granted by the ethical committee of the Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences at Ghent University with reference number 2025-091A.
live_data_statements: Participants were native English speakers, recruited via Prolific Academic.
Based on the given premises and reversal statement, participants had to select all buttons with true or false statements from 2-to-4 buttons.

Trials differed based on whether participants had to indicate true or false statements, the number of buttons (2, 3, 4), and the number of true (none true, one true, two true) vs. false (none false, one false, two false, three false) statements.
If participants had not clicked the submit button before the response deadline of 80 seconds, no response was registered, and the next trial started immediately.
There was no response deadline, but participants were instructed to react as fast and accurately as possible.
At the start of the study, participants provided informed consent and demographic information, including age and gender ("male," "female," "non-binary," "not listed," or "prefer not to say").
After the DR task, participants completed the VPT task and Faux Pas Recognition Test, for which the order was randomized across participants.
After both tasks, participants completed the ICAR Sample Test and the AQ-Short.
Finally, participants were debriefed and informed that they could contact the researcher via Prolific if they had any questions or would like to receive a summary of the results.
Participants were also given the option to leave a comment before finishing the study.
Eight participants were excluded because they failed more than one out of the four attention checks during the experiment.

Four additional participants were excluded because they had more than 20% trials with RTs ≤ 5 seconds during the DR task (1 participant) or because their average accuracy in the VPT task was ≤ 57% (3 participants).
Participants had an average score of 60.47% (SD = 24.39%) on the DR task.
Participants were faster (Mraw RT difference = 358 ms, SD = 527 ms) and more accurate (Mdifference = 6.75%, SD = 9.59%) on congruent compared to incongruent trials.
Participants had an average accuracy of 55.26% (SD = 19.69%) on the ICAR Sample Test.

In our previous research using Prolific samples, up to 11% of participants also scored above the 50-item AQ cut-off (Nevejans et al., 2026; Experiment 1), suggesting a possible selection bias toward individuals with elevated autism traits on Prolific, at least for this type of research.
After each block, participants were informed about their average accuracy in the finished block.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 9 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:9, File = c("power_simulation.R", "preprocessing.qmd", 
"processing_pilot.qmd", "processing.qmd", "processing.R", "analysis_confirmatory.qmd", 
"analysis_confirmatory.R", "analysis_meta_analysis.qmd", "analysis_posthoc.qmd"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "preprocessing.qmd", 
"preprocessing.qmd", "processing.qmd, processing.R", "processing.qmd, processing.R, analysis_confirmatory.qmd", 
"processing.qmd, processing.R", "processing.qmd, processing.R"
), Basis = c("none", "none", "none", "dependency", "dependency", 
"dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency")), row.names = c(NA, 
-9L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 3 data files that are not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `deictic_task.csv`, `vpt_task_simdata.csv`, `pilot_fauxpas_task.csv`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 9 scripts: 5 ran without error, 3 errored, 1 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script uses an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `analysis_confirmatory.R` after `analysis_confirmatory.qmd`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. **A script looked for a file in another folder than the deposit has it**, so before running it once more we copied it there: `pilot study/raw/raw.csv` to `data/raw/raw.csv` for `preprocessing.qmd`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this. 

*a script hit an `object '...' not found` error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first, and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

> corrected_vpt_splitHalf <- function(sims = 1){
>    
>    corrected_corsplits <- replicate(sims, { # this is the simulation
>       
>       vpt_with_ranrow <- vpt_processed.df %>% 
>          # We order the full task based on conditions, to get a balanced split-sample of trials (= conditions in each half)
>          select(pp_number, vpt_angle, vpt_congruency, vpt_correct_resp, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_pos_red, vpt_distance, vpt_trial_number, vpt_trial_accuracy, duration) %>%
>          arrange(pp_number, vpt_distance, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_correct_resp, vpt_congruency, vpt_trial_number) %>% # arrange the rows per condition
>          group_by(pp_number, vpt_distance, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_correct_resp, vpt_congruency) %>%
>          mutate(row_random = sample(row_number(), replace = F)) %>% # give each row a number within each relevant condition
>          arrange(pp_number, vpt_distance, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_correct_resp, vpt_congruency, row_random) %>%
>          mutate(split = ifelse(row_random %% 2 == 0, 2, 1)) # odd numbers in one half, even in the other; somewhat equal halves
>       
>       vtp_split1 <- vpt_with_ranrow %>% filter(split == 1) # one half 
>       
>       vtp_split2 <- vpt_with_ranrow %>% filter(split == 2) # another half
>       
>       # And calculate the congruency effect for each split (same code as above)
>       rce_s1 <- vtp_split1 %>%
>          group_by(pp_number,
>                   vpt_angle, vpt_congruency, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_pos_red, vpt_distance) %>% # congruency within different conditions
>          summarise(marginal_rt = mean(duration)) %>%
>          group_by(pp_number, vpt_congruency) %>%
>          summarise(mean_rt = mean(marginal_rt)) %>%
>          spread(vpt_congruency, mean_rt) %>%
>          mutate(vpt_rel_ce_rt = (incongruent - congruent)/((incongruent+congruent)/2)) %>% # we divide by the average speed for each participant
>          ungroup() %>%
>          select(pp_number, vpt_rel_ce_rt) 
>       
>       rce_s2 <- vtp_split2 %>%
>          group_by(pp_number,
>                   vpt_angle, vpt_congruency, vpt_presentation_half, vpt_pos_red, vpt_distance) %>% # congruency within different conditions
>          summarise(marginal_rt = mean(duration)) %>%
>          group_by(pp_number, vpt_congruency) %>%
>          summarise(mean_rt = mean(marginal_rt)) %>%
>          spread(vpt_congruency, mean_rt) %>%
>          mutate(vpt_rel_ce_rt = (incongruent - congruent)/((incongruent+congruent)/2)) %>% # we divide by the average speed for each participant
>          ungroup() %>%
>          select(pp_number, vpt_rel_ce_rt) 
>       
>       #Finally, we correlate the congruency effects in these splits, and Spearman-Brown correct it 
>       cor_splits <- cor(rce_s1$vpt_rel_ce_rt, rce_s2$vpt_rel_ce_rt, method = "pearson")
>       
>       corrected_split_cor <- (2*cor_splits)/(1 + cor_splits) #Spearman-Brown corrected
>       corrected_split_cor
>       
>    })
>    
>    quantile(corrected_corsplits, probs = c(0.025, 0.50, 0.975)) # from the lest of correlations, take these values
> }
> corrected_vpt_splitHalf(sims = 10000)

text.text: Relational Frame Theory (RFT) proposes that deictic relating plays a critical role in "Theory of Mind" (ToM).

However, empirical research to date on the relationship between deictic relating and ToM has been inconclusive, potentially due to small sample sizes and limitations in the assessment of deictic relating.

In the present online study (N = 164), we tested the relationship between deictic relating and two ToM measures: a low-level ToM task (a visual perspective-taking task) and a high-level ToM task (the Faux Pas Recognition Test).
We additionally tested associations with general cognitive ability and autism traits.
Based on predictions from RFT, we hypothesized that deictic relating would correlate with both ToM measures, with a stronger association for low-level ToM.

We observed a positive correlation of deictic relating with performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test, whereas its correlation with visual perspective-taking was non-significant for our primary outcome measure.

Opposite to predictions derived from RFT, deictic relating was positively correlated with autism traits, whereas scores on the Faux Pas Recognition Test and visual perspective-taking task were not significantly correlated with autism traits.
Although these findings may suggest a relationship between deictic relating and ToM, the absence of an association with low-level ToM is difficult to reconcile with RFT.
Alternative explanations for observed correlations, including task characteristics or other related abilities, are discussed.
Finally, the finding that higher scores on the autism traits questionnaire were related to better deictic relating is at odds with RFT and raises questions about which abilities the task measures.

Theory of Mind (ToM), typically defined as the ability to attribute mental states to oneself and others (Premack & Woodruff, 1978), is argued to be crucial for successful social interaction (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985; Leslie et al., 2004; Long et al., 2025; Todd & Galinsky, 2014).
text.formatted: Theory of Mind (ToM), typically defined as the ability to attribute mental states to oneself and others <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Premack & Woodruff, 1978)</ref>, is argued to be crucial for successful social interaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baron-Cohen et al., 1985;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Leslie et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Long et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Todd & Galinsky, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: ToM has been investigated in many subfields of cognitive psychology (Schaafsma et al., 2015) and can therefore be seen as an "umbrella term" encompassing several related abilities. Howlin et al. (1999) classified these ToM abilities into five developmental levels of increasing complexity.
text.formatted: ToM has been investigated in many subfields of cognitive psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Schaafsma et al., 2015)</ref> and can therefore be seen as an "umbrella term" encompassing several related abilities. <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Howlin et al. (1999)</ref> classified these ToM abilities into five developmental levels of increasing complexity.

text.text: The first two levels, simple and complex visual perspective-taking (VPT), reflect the understanding that different people can see different things (level 1) or the same thing differently (level 2).
Level 3 refers to the understanding that individuals can only know what they have (in)directly experienced, also named "seeing leads to knowing".

Finally, levels 4 and 5, considered to be the most complex ToM levels, involve predicting actions based on a person's true (level 4) or false (level 5) beliefs (Howlin et al., 1999; Montoya-Rodríguez & Cobos, 2016).
text.formatted: Finally, levels 4 and 5, considered to be the most complex ToM levels, involve predicting actions based on a person's true (level 4) or false (level 5) beliefs <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Howlin et al., 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Montoya-Rodríguez & Cobos, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, it remains unclear whether these different abilities indeed rely on a single underlying "ToM process" or instead reflect distinct cognitive processes (Brucato et al., 2026; Quesque & Rossetti, 2020; Schaafsma et al., 2015).
text.formatted: However, it remains unclear whether these different abilities indeed rely on a single underlying "ToM process" or instead reflect distinct cognitive processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Brucato et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Quesque & Rossetti, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Schaafsma et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Relational Frame Theory (RFT; Hayes et al., 2001) provides an alternative, behavioranalytic view of ToM abilities through the concept of deictic relating (DR), a specific type of relational responding.
text.formatted: Relational Frame Theory (RFT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Hayes et al., 2001)</ref> provides an alternative, behavioranalytic view of ToM abilities through the concept of deictic relating (DR), a specific type of relational responding.

text.text: RFT proposes that relational responding lies at the core of human cognition and language, and distinguishes different types of relating, referred to as relational frames, such as frames of coordination (e.g., A is the same as B), opposition (e.g., A is opposite to B), or temporality (e.g., A comes after B).

Perspective-taking is assumed to involve responding to a family of deictic frames, including three key deictic relations: interpersonal relations (I versus YOU), spatial relations (HERE versus THERE), and temporal relations (NOW versus THEN).
text.formatted: Perspective-taking is assumed to involve responding to a family of deictic frames, including three key deictic relations: interpersonal relations (I versus YOU), spatial relations (HERE versus THERE), and temporal relations <ref type="bibr">(NOW versus THEN)</ref>.

text.text: According to RFT, DR develops through a history of reinforcement to responding to questions involving these critical relations, such as "What are you doing right now?", "What did you eat at school today?", or "What did your sister do this morning?"

Responding to such questions requires children to distinguish their own perspective in the "here" and "now" from other perspectives, including those of another person (e.g., "their sister"), at a different place (e.g., "at school"), and at a different time (e.g., "this morning").

Repeatedly making such distinctions across contexts allows children to abstract the underlying relational properties, through which they learn to describe their own perspective in relation to others (Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004; McHugh et al., 2004; Rehfeldt et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Repeatedly making such distinctions across contexts allows children to abstract the underlying relational properties, through which they learn to describe their own perspective in relation to others <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">McHugh et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Rehfeldt et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: RFT researchers have claimed that DR represents the essential behavioral repertoire for ToM abilities described in cognitive psychology (Hempkin et al., 2024), although some claim that, whereas DR would be heavily involved in levels 1-to-3 of ToM, higher levels (and especially false-belief reasoning) might involve more than DR, such as logical-not reasoning (e.g., "you were NOT here"; Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004) or relating of relational networks (Kavanagh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: RFT researchers have claimed that DR represents the essential behavioral repertoire for ToM abilities described in cognitive psychology <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hempkin et al., 2024)</ref>, although some claim that, whereas DR would be heavily involved in levels 1-to-3 of ToM, higher levels (and especially false-belief reasoning) might involve more than DR, such as logical-not reasoning (e.g., "you were NOT here"; <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004)</ref> or relating of relational networks <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kavanagh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Based on the assumed link between DR and ToM, several studies within RFT have tested whether training individuals on DR also improves performance on ToM tasks, with the aim of eventually applying such training to populations thought to experience ToM difficulties, such as individuals with autismfoot_0  (Lovett & Rehfeldt, 2014).
text.formatted: Based on the assumed link between DR and ToM, several studies within RFT have tested whether training individuals on DR also improves performance on ToM tasks, with the aim of eventually applying such training to populations thought to experience ToM difficulties, such as individuals with autism<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref>  <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Lovett & Rehfeldt, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: To do so, researchers typically use the so-called "Barnes-Holmes protocol" (see McHugh et al., 2004) to assess and train DR across three levels of relational complexity: simple, reversed, and double reversed.
text.formatted: To do so, researchers typically use the so-called "Barnes-Holmes protocol" (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">McHugh et al., 2004)</ref> to assess and train DR across three levels of relational complexity: simple, reversed, and double reversed.

text.text: In each trial of this protocol, the researcher gives the participant certain information involving deictic relations, such as "I am sitting here on the black chair and you are sitting there on the blue chair," after which the participant must answer two questions, for example, "Where am I sitting?
Where are you sitting?"
Crucially, deictic relational information can be "reversed" in certain trials through an additional statement, such as "If I were you and you were me" (an interpersonal reversal).

A double reversal statement, considered to have the highest relational complexity, could be "If now were then and then were now, and if here were there and there were here", in which both the temporal and spatial deictic relations are reversed (Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004; Rehfeldt et al., 2007).
text.formatted: A double reversal statement, considered to have the highest relational complexity, could be "If now were then and then were now, and if here were there and there were here", in which both the temporal and spatial deictic relations are reversed <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Rehfeldt et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Studies using the Barnes-Holmes protocol to investigate transfer of DR training to ToM task performance have, however, provided mixed results.

Some studies reported (descriptive) improvements on level 3 to 5 ToM tasks following DR training in typically developing children (Weil et al., 2011), adolescents with autism (Lovett & Rehfeldt, 2014), and adults with schizophrenia (O'Neill & Weil, 2014).

text.text: However, other studies have found no such improvements on ToM tests across all five levels in typically developing children (Montoya-Rodríguez & Cobos, 2016) or children with autism (Jackson et al., 2014).
text.formatted: However, other studies have found no such improvements on ToM tests across all five levels in typically developing children <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Montoya-Rodríguez & Cobos, 2016)</ref> or children with autism <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Jackson et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, all these studies had very small sample sizes, with no more than three participants in the training group, and relied on descriptive comparisons of accuracy scores rather than statistical inference tests.

Although behavior analysis has historically used such descriptive analyses informatively, this is in the context of single-case experimental designs; the above studies, by contrast, largely focus on designs that are closer to typical group-level approaches, which are less appropriate for such descriptive analyses (Cummins, 2026).

text.text: More recently, Taylor et al. (2023) addressed these limitations by recruiting a larger adult sample and including an active control group.

text.text: They found no transfer of DR training to performance on a VPT task, nor to an implicit relational assessment procedure intended to measure perspective-taking within an RFT framework.

A recent scoping review on the relationship between ToM and DR in autism reached a similar conclusion, stating that there is currently insufficient evidence for improvements in ToM performance after DR training (Hempkin et al., 2024).

text.text: Hence, it remains unclear whether DR is related to ToM performance, particularly in the general adult population.
The current study tested the relationship between DR performance and a low-and high-level ToM task in a large adult sample, thereby addressing the limited sample sizes in most previous studies.
Aside from sample size limitations, the Barnes-Holmes protocol might also be a suboptimal measure of DR performance, especially in adults.

Indeed, the protocol was originally designed to train children with lower DR abilities (Kavanagh et al., 2020), and it is therefore unclear whether the protocol has sufficient variation in difficulty to assess performance in adults.

text.text: To assess both low-and high-level ToM, we included a level-2 VPT task (Huang et al., 2026) and the Faux Pas Recognition Test (level 5 ToM; Burghardt et al., 2025; Stone et al., 1998).

text.text: We further included a measure of cognitive abilities and an assessment of autism traits.

First, given that both ToM (Baker et al., 2014; Navarro et al., 2021) and DR (Gore et al., 2010) have been shown to correlate with intelligence measures, observed relationships may be (partially) driven by general cognitive ability.

text.text: Second, because ToM (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985; Long et al., 2025) and DR (Hempkin et al., 2024; Rehfeldt et al., 2007) have been linked to autism, we included a self-report questionnaire of autism traits, the shortened version of the Autism Spectrum Quotient (AQ-Short; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Hoekstra et al., 2011), to test the relationship between performance on the tasks and autism traits in the general population.

text.text: We tested two primary hypotheses about the relationship between DR and ToM.

Based on RFT, our first primary hypothesis (H1) was that DR performance would be positively associated with VPT; our second primary hypothesis (H2) was that DR performance would be positively associated with performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test.

However, because some theorists have argued that DR alone may be insufficient to support higher-level ToM abilities (Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004; Kavanagh et al., 2020), we added the secondary hypothesis that DR would be more strongly associated with VPT than with performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test.

text.text: Additionally, we tested the relationship between autism traits and performance on the DR and ToM tasks.

The ToM hypothesis of autism states that individuals with autism should perform worse on ToM tasks (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985), and previous research has linked autism traits to lower ToM scores (Atherton & Cross, 2019; Gökçen et al., 2016; Nijhof et al., 2017).

text.text: Based on such previous claims within RFT, we would hence expect a negative correlation between autism traits and DR performance.
However, a previous study with the novel DR task in a large general sample did not observe any correlation between autism traits and performance on DR (Nevejans et al., 2026).

text.text: The current study therefore aimed to test whether the predicted negative correlation is observed or whether the previous null result is replicated.

text.text: To determine the minimum required sample size, we conducted a simulation-based power analysis for the two main hypotheses (H1, H2).
For both power analyses, we simulated data based on two previous studies (Huang et al., 2026; Nevejans et al., 2026) and a pilot study on the Faux Pas Recognition Test.

Once 164 complete submissions had been collected, data were screened for exclusion criteria (see Analysis section), and excluded submissions were replaced through additional recruitment.
This process was repeated until we obtained the preregistered sample size from the power analysis (N = 164).
In total, 176 complete submissions were collected, of which 164 participants (87 female, 76 male, 1 "not listed", Mage = 30.63, SDage = 5.36) were included in the final analysis sample.
The DR task included 24 trials and two attention checks, with a break after 12 trials.
Apart from the attention checks, which had a fixed trial number, all trials appeared in random order.
On each trial, participants read two premises, each describing "I" or "you" doing or feeling something at a certain place and time.
The two premises always described a different person, place, and time.
An example combination of premises could be "You were rollerblading on the sidewalk two days ago; I am stretching in the sports center right now" (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: An example combination of premises could be "You were rollerblading on the sidewalk two days ago; I am stretching in the sports center right now" (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Half of the trials included two premises about actions (action trials), whereas the other half included two premises about feelings (emotion trials).

Below the premises, participants read a reversal statement, which could include an interpersonal ("If I were you and you were me"), spatial (e.g., "If the sidewalk were the sports center, and the sports center were the sidewalk"), or temporal (e.g., "If now were two days ago and two days ago were now") deictic reversal, or a combination of two reversals (i.e., a double-reversal), resulting in six possible reversals.
This created a 2-by-6 task design, in which the trial type (action trial, emotion trial) and reversal (six possible reversals) varied.
Based on the given premises and reversal statement, participants had to select all buttons with true or false statements from 2-to-4 buttons.

Trials differed based on whether participants had to indicate true or false statements, the number of buttons (2, 3, 4), and the number of true (none true, one true, two true) vs. false (none false, one false, two false, three false) statements.
There was always at least one correct option.
If participants had not clicked the submit button before the response deadline of 80 seconds, no response was registered, and the next trial started immediately.

text.text: Each trial started with a 700 ms inter-trial interval, showing a white "+" on a black background.
After this period, participants observed an image of an avatar standing at a round table on which two balls were placed next to each other, a red and a yellow ball.
Participants reacted to the left-right position of the red ball from the avatar's perspective by pressing the F-or J-key, corresponding to the responses "left" and "right" respectively.
There was no response deadline, but participants were instructed to react as fast and accurately as possible.
The next trial immediately started after the participant's response.
In each trial, the avatar's perspective could be congruent or incongruent with the participant's perspective.
More specifically, the avatar could be placed at different angles (i.e., positions) around the table, with a 0° angle corresponding to the participant's perspective.

The translations were then checked by a native English speaker, after which we adjusted some items for clarity.

We further used the original stories and questions from the English openformat Faux Pas Recognition Test for adults (Stone et al., 1998), rather than the German version, which was itself a translation of the original materials.

text.text: In this task, participants read 20 short stories (taken from Stone et al., 1998), presented in a fixed order: 10 stories contained a faux pas (faux pas stories) and 10 stories did not (control stories).
text.formatted: In this task, participants read 20 short stories (taken from <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Stone et al., 1998)</ref>, presented in a fixed order: 10 stories contained a faux pas (faux pas stories) and 10 stories did not (control stories).

text.text: After reading a story, participants first received a yes-no question (Q1): "In the story, did anyone say something they shouldn't have said or something awkward?"

If they indicated "yes" to this question, they had to answer three additional questions, namely, (Q2) "Who said something they shouldn't have said or something awkward?", (Q3) "Why do you think he/she said it?", and (Q4) "How do you think […] felt?", in which the blank was filled in by another character in the story.
For faux pas stories, this was always the "victim" of the faux pas.
If participants indicated "no" to the first question, questions 2, 3, and 4 were skipped for that story.
Questions 2, 3, and 4 always had four response options.
For each story, participants also completed two comprehension questions about the content of the story.
Comprehension questions could have between 2 and 4 response options.
The written story remained on the screen for all questions, and participants could not go back to previous questions.

The ICAR Sample Test (Condon & Revelle, 2014) is a shortened version of the ICAR Test (The International Cognitive Ability Resource Team, 2014) and includes four subscales, each including four items from the ICAR: Verbal Reasoning (items 4, 16, 17, and 19), Letter and Number Series (items 7, 33, 34, 58), Matrix Reasoning (items 45, 46, 47, 55), and Three-Dimensional Rotation (items 3, 4, 6, 8).
text.formatted: The ICAR Sample Test <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Condon & Revelle, 2014)</ref> is a shortened version of the ICAR Test (The International Cognitive Ability Resource Team, 2014) and includes four subscales, each including four items from the ICAR: Verbal Reasoning (items 4, 16, 17, and 19), Letter and Number Series (items 7, 33, 34, 58), Matrix Reasoning (items 45, 46, 47, 55), and Three-Dimensional Rotation (items 3, 4, 6, 8).

text.text: The items were presented one by one in a fixed order.
Each item appeared on a separate screen during the experiment, and participants could not go back to previous questions.

The AQ-Short (Hoekstra et al., 2011) contains 28 items from the full AQ (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001) divided into five subscales: social skills (8 items), imagination (8 items), routines (3 items), attention to numbers and patterns (5 items), and attention switching (4 items).
text.formatted: The AQ-Short <ref type="bibr">(Hoekstra et al., 2011</ref>) contains 28 items from the full AQ <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Baron-Cohen et al., 2001)</ref> divided into five subscales: social skills (8 items), imagination (8 items), routines (3 items), attention to numbers and patterns (5 items), and attention switching (4 items).

text.text: Participants indicated how much they agreed with each statement on a four-point Likert scale, with the options "definitely disagree", "disagree", "agree", and "definitely agree".
The AQ-Short was scored following Hoekstra et al. (2011), with item scores ranging from 1 (definitely disagree) to 4 (definitely agree).
text.formatted: The AQ-Short was scored following <ref type="bibr">Hoekstra et al. (2011)</ref>, with item scores ranging from 1 (definitely disagree) to 4 (definitely agree).

text.text: At the start of the study, participants provided informed consent and demographic information, including age and gender ("male," "female," "non-binary," "not listed," or "prefer not to say").
Participants who selected "not listed" could specify an alternative gender.
Participants first completed the DR task, for which they first completed three practice trials with elaborate feedback for incorrect responses.
After the DR task, participants completed the VPT task and Faux Pas Recognition Test, for which the order was randomized across participants.
The presentation order was roughly balanced across participants, with 85 (52%) participants completing the VPT task first and 79 (48%) participants completing the Faux Pas Recognition Test first.
For the VPT task, participants first completed a practice block with twelve trials, which was repeated until they had an accuracy of at least 75% (correct on 9 out of 12 trials).
The Faux Pas Recognition Test did not include any practice trials.
After both tasks, participants completed the ICAR Sample Test and the AQ-Short.
Finally, participants were debriefed and informed that they could contact the researcher via Prolific if they had any questions or would like to receive a summary of the results.
Participants were also given the option to leave a comment before finishing the study.
All data were processed and analyzed using R (Version 4.5.2; R Core Team, 2023).
Participant and trial exclusions followed the preregistered plan.
The DR Task.

In line with previous research, a trial in the DR task was coded as correct if all correct statements (i.e., either all false or all true statements, depending on the instruction) were selected and all incorrect statements were unselected.
A trial was coded as incorrect if participants made one or more mistakes or did not press the submit button before the trial deadline.
Our outcome measure for the DR task was the average accuracy across all 24 trials.
The VPT Task.

As VPT tasks typically show ceiling effects on accuracy (e.g., Huang et al., 2026; Kessler & Rutherford, 2010; Michelon & Zacks, 2006), we chose to use the congruency effect on the reaction times (RTs) as our main outcome measure.
text.formatted: As VPT tasks typically show ceiling effects on accuracy (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Huang et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Kessler & Rutherford, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Michelon & Zacks, 2006)</ref>, we chose to use the congruency effect on the reaction times (RTs) as our main outcome measure.

text.text: This was calculated by subtracting the participant's mean RT on (correct) congruent trials from their mean RT on (correct) incongruent trials (which corresponds to the "visual congruency" effect in Huang et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This was calculated by subtracting the participant's mean RT on (correct) congruent trials from their mean RT on (correct) incongruent trials (which corresponds to the "visual congruency" effect in <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Huang et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Because congruency effects often scale with general RT, it is recommended to control for overall RT to reduce the potential for misinterpreting congruency effects (Faust et al., 1999).
text.formatted: Because congruency effects often scale with general RT, it is recommended to control for overall RT to reduce the potential for misinterpreting congruency effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Faust et al., 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, we divided the congruency effect by the participant's overall mean RT to obtain a "relative" congruency effect for each participantfoot_2 : .

text.text: The Faux Pas Recognition Test.
We based our score calculation on the study by Burghardt et al. (2025), who recommended using only the empathy and the intention scores suggested by Stone et al. (1998).
text.formatted: We based our score calculation on the study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Burghardt et al. (2025)</ref>, who recommended using only the empathy and the intention scores suggested by <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Stone et al. (1998)</ref>.

text.text: To calculate a participant's score, stories with one or two incorrect comprehension questions were first excluded.
The scoring of the intention and empathy questions depended on whether the participant answered the first question correctly.
For faux pas stories, the intention question was scored as correct if the participant selected the correct response on the intention question (Q3) after identifying a faux pas in Q1.
For control stories, the intention question was scored as correct if the participant correctly indicated that no faux pas had occurred in Q1, in which case Q3 was not presented.
If a participant responded incorrectly to Q1, the intention question was always scored as incorrect.
The empathy question (Q4) was scored as correct if participants selected the correct response on Q4, regardless of whether they answered Q1 correctly.
For control stories, the empathy question was also scored as correct if participants correctly indicated in Q1 that no faux pas had occurred, in which case Q4 was not presented.

The empathy question was scored as incorrect if participants failed to identify a faux pas in Q1 for faux pas stories (resulting in Q4 not being presented) or if they selected an incorrect emotion on Q4.
Regarding the calculation of the total intention and empathy score, Burghardt et al.
(2025) recommended not dividing the total scores by the number of correctly answered comprehension questions.

However, because we aimed to assess accuracy on empathy and intention questions, independent of comprehension, we chose to take the average score across all included stories (i.e., stories with correct comprehension questions).

The intention score was calculated by taking the average score on the intention questions across all included stories, and the empathy score was calculated by taking the average score on all empathy questions for included stories.
We used the sum of the intention and empathy score, ranging from 0 to 2, as the total score for the Faux Pas Recognition Test.
Participant Exclusions.
Only participants with complete data (> 80%) on the DR task, the VPT task, and the Faux Pas Recognition Test were included in the analysis.
text.formatted: Only participants with complete data (> 80%) on the DR task, the VPT task, and the Faux Pas Recognition Test were included in the analysis.

text.text: Eight participants were excluded because they failed more than one out of the four attention checks during the experiment.

Four additional participants were excluded because they had more than 20% trials with RTs ≤ 5 seconds during the DR task (1 participant) or because their average accuracy in the VPT task was ≤ 57% (3 participants).
This accuracy threshold corresponds to the 97.5th percentile of a binomial distribution with 192 trials and a success probability of 0.5, with the corresponding lower bound at 43% (2.5th percentile).
Accuracy scores between these values may reflect random responding.
Because the RT congruency effect on the VPT task was calculated based on correct trials only, we applied a one-sided threshold.

In the Faux Pas Recognition Test, all questions for a story were excluded if the participant responded incorrectly to one or more of the comprehension questions for that story (4.45% of the stories were excluded across all participants).
In the VPT task, trials were excluded from all analyses if the log-transformed RT ≥ 3SD above or below the participant's average log-transformed RT (1% of trials were excluded).
We used log-transformed RTs to approximate a normal distribution.
VPT task trials with incorrect responses were removed for the relative RT congruency effect calculation (4.49%).

As preregistered, we computed Spearman's rank-ordered correlations between (H1) accuracy on the DR task and the relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task, and between (H2) accuracy on the DR task and the summed intention-empathy score on the Faux Pas Recognition Test.
We report the corresponding 95% CIs and raw p values.
We computed Bayes Factors (BF) for the correlations of interest using Jeffrey's default BF hypothesis test (Ly et al., 2016), available in the BayesFactor package in R (Morey et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We computed Bayes Factors (BF) for the correlations of interest using Jeffrey's default BF hypothesis test <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Ly et al., 2016)</ref>, available in the BayesFactor package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Morey et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Difference in the Correlation Between DR and Low-vs.
High-Level ToM.

We tested whether the Spearman correlation between DR accuracy scores and the relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task significantly differed from the correlation between the DR accuracy scores and the summed intention-empathy score, using the cocor package in R. As we aimed to test differences in strength, we aligned the correlations to the same direction by reversing negative correlations (if there were any).
We expected a stronger correlation with the relative RT congruency effect compared to the summed intention-empathy score.
We computed Spearman accuracy on the DR task, their relative RT congruency effect on the VPT task, and their summed intention-empathy score on the Faux Pas Recognition Test.
We report adjusted p values and corrected 95% CIs using the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure for controlling the False Discovery Rate (FDR).

Finally, we also computed Spearman correlations between participants' AQ-Short scores and their accuracy on the DR task, their relative VPT RT congruency effect, and their summed intention-empathy score on the Faux Pas Recognition Test.
We report adjusted p values and corrected 95% CIs using the BH procedure.

We preregistered that we would also calculate the correlations between AQ scores and all specific Faux Pas Recognition Test scores, for which the analysis and results can be found in the Supplementary Materials (Appendix A).
