Previous research on the relationship between DR and ToM has been mixed, potentially due to small sample sizes (e.g., Jackson et al., 2014; Weil et al., 2011) and the limited applicability of the Barnes-Holmes protocol for adults (Kavanagh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Previous research on the relationship between DR and ToM has been mixed, potentially due to small sample sizes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Jackson et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Weil et al., 2011)</ref> and the limited applicability of the Barnes-Holmes protocol for adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kavanagh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: The current study tested correlations between performance on a recently developed DR task suitable for adults and a low-and high-level ToM task, namely a VPT task and the Faux Pas Recognition Test, in a large general population sample.
We further tested correlations with a measure of cognitive abilities, the ICAR Sample Test, and a self-report questionnaire of autism traits, the AQ-Short.
Contrary to H1, DR performance was not significantly correlated with our low-level ToM measure, the RT congruency effect in the VPT task.
However, DR was significantly correlated with our high-level ToM measure, the summed intention-empathy score, consistent with H2.
The correlation with high-level ToM was significantly stronger than with low-level ToM, which was opposite to what would be predicted by RFT.
In a secondary analysis, we found significant correlations of the ICAR Sample Test with both DR and the summed intention-empathy scores.
Furthermore, autism traits were positively correlated with DR, although they were not significantly correlated with the summed intention-empathy scores and VPT RT congruency effect.
Hence, contrary to our predictions, higher autism trait scores were associated with higher accuracy on the DR task, and were not significantly associated with performance on our ToM tasks.

Because the summed intention-empathy score correlated with both DR and ICAR scores, and RFT predicts that DR should relate to Faux Pas performance beyond general cognitive ability, we conducted a post-hoc analysis to test whether DR scores still correlated with the summed intention-empathy scores when controlling for ICAR scores.
In line with RFT's prediction, the analysis revealed a significant partial correlation between DR and summed intention-empathy scores after controlling for ICAR scores.
This suggests that the relation between DR and performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test cannot be fully explained by general cognitive ability.
Regarding H1, a possible explanation for the absence of a significant correlation with VPT is that this was the only outcome based on RTs, whereas the other outcome measures were accuracy scores.
To test this, we performed a post-hoc correlational analysis with the accuracy congruency effect instead of the RT congruency effect.
This analysis revealed small but significant negative correlations with DR and ICAR scores.
That is, higher DR and ICAR scores were related to smaller accuracy congruency effects in the VPT task.

The negative correlation with DR is in line with RFT's prediction, as the congruency effect reflects a cost for perspective switching (i.e., lower accuracy for incongruent vs. congruent perspectives); a smaller congruency effect therefore indicates less difficulty with switching perspectives.

However, the non-significant partial correlation between DR and VPT after controlling for ICAR scores suggests that the observed correlation with the DR task may reflect general cognitive ability rather than a specific link between DR and VPT.

The absence of a unique association aligns with Taylor et al. (2023), who found no effect of DR training on VPT performance; if observed associations are solely driven by cognitive ability, specific DR training is unlikely to transfer to VPT.
text.formatted: The absence of a unique association aligns with <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Taylor et al. (2023)</ref>, who found no effect of DR training on VPT performance; if observed associations are solely driven by cognitive ability, specific DR training is unlikely to transfer to VPT.

text.text: Moreover, RFT further assumes low-level ToM to rely more directly on DR compared to high-level ToM (Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004; Kavanagh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Moreover, RFT further assumes low-level ToM to rely more directly on DR compared to high-level ToM <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kavanagh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, these findings for low-level ToM are at odds with RFT's predictions.
However, we did find a correlation between DR and high-level ToM.

The observed correlation between DR and the Faux Pas Recognition Test is consistent with previous correlational research reporting correlations between DR and vignette-based high-level ToM tasks (Hendriks et al., 2016; Villatte et al., 2008 Villatte et al., , 2010)).
text.formatted: The observed correlation between DR and the Faux Pas Recognition Test is consistent with previous correlational research reporting correlations between DR and vignette-based high-level ToM tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hendriks et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Villatte et al., 2008</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Villatte et al., , 2010))</ref>.

text.text: However, several alternative explanations for the relationship between the two tasks must be considered.
First, we observed a stronger correlation between DR and high-level ToM compared to low-level ToM.
Importantly, our low-and high-level ToM tasks differed not only in ToM level but also in task format: the VPT task was non-verbal, whereas both the DR and Faux Pas Recognition
Test were text-based.

Moreover, the Faux Pas Recognition Test and DR task both rely on active reasoning (i.e., reading certain statements or stories, and answering questions about their content), which is likely more cognitively demanding than simply overcoming one's own visual perspective in a two-choice, trial-based task.
Hence, the relationship between DR and the Faux Pas Recognition Test may partly reflect shared task characteristics and reliance on active reasoning rather than a link between DR and ToM abilities.
Using the same logic, it is also possible that DR did not significantly correlate with VPT (beyond cognitive ability) because these tasks differ (too much) in format.
Therefore, task-specific variance may have obscured a potential association between VPT and DR.

To investigate task-specific influences, future research could include tasks with other task formats, such as a non-verbal high-level ToM task (e.g., Nijhof et al., 2017), or add a cognitive non-social task with overlapping task structure and difficulty.
text.formatted: To investigate task-specific influences, future research could include tasks with other task formats, such as a non-verbal high-level ToM task (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Nijhof et al., 2017)</ref>, or add a cognitive non-social task with overlapping task structure and difficulty.

text.text: Relatedly, because of the overlap in task structure, the observed correlation may (partly) reflect a third underlying ability assessed in both the DR task and the Faux Pas Recognition Test other than perspective-taking.
One possibility is verbal ability, as language skills have been linked to ToM performance (Astington & Jenkins, 1999; Milligan et al., 2007; Navarro et al., 2021) as well as DR (Gore et al., 2010).
text.formatted: One possibility is verbal ability, as language skills have been linked to ToM performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Astington & Jenkins, 1999;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Milligan et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Navarro et al., 2021)</ref> as well as DR <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Gore et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, RFT states that relational responding is essential to language development (Hayes et al., 2001), and critiques of DR have argued that the Barnes-Holmes protocol may function as training in complex sentence structures rather than perspective-taking (Taylor & Edwards, 2021).
text.formatted: Moreover, RFT states that relational responding is essential to language development <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hayes et al., 2001)</ref>, and critiques of DR have argued that the Barnes-Holmes protocol may function as training in complex sentence structures rather than perspective-taking <ref type="bibr">(Taylor & Edwards, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Although the ICAR Sample Test includes a verbal reasoning subscale, it comprises only four items and may therefore provide a limited assessment of verbal ability.
Hence, whereas ICAR scores did not fully explain the correlation between DR and the Faux Pas Recognition Test, a more comprehensive test of verbal ability might.

These alternative explanations of the observed correlation between DR and the Faux Pas Recognition Test are not only relevant to the current study, but may also explain previously reported correlations between performance on the Barnes-Holmes protocol and vignette-based ToM tasks (Hendriks et al., 2016; Villatte et al., 2008 Villatte et al., , 2010)).
text.formatted: These alternative explanations of the observed correlation between DR and the Faux Pas Recognition Test are not only relevant to the current study, but may also explain previously reported correlations between performance on the Barnes-Holmes protocol and vignette-based ToM tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Hendriks et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Villatte et al., 2008</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Villatte et al., , 2010))</ref>.

text.text: Future research could include a more comprehensive measure of language skills to determine whether the observed association persists when taking into account verbal ability.
It is also possible that the observed correlation reflects a relationship between ToM and relational responding more generally, rather than a specific association with DR.
Because DR is thought to be specifically related to ToM development, ToM should show a stronger association with DR than with other relational frames.
To test the specificity of the relationship, future studies could include additional measures of (non-deictic) relational responding.

One measure could be the analogy subscale in the improved Relational Abilities Index (J. Cummins & J. De Houwer, personal communication, June 2024; Nevejans et al., 2026), which closely matches the DR task in structure and difficulty.
text.formatted: One measure could be the analogy subscale in the improved Relational Abilities Index (J. <ref type="bibr">Cummins & J. De Houwer, personal communication, June 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Nevejans et al., 2026)</ref>, which closely matches the DR task in structure and difficulty.

text.text: If ToM correlates more strongly with DR than with other relational frames, this would provide stronger evidence that its correlation is not solely based on relational abilities in general or overlap in task structure.

Regarding our secondary analysis, the lack of a significant correlation between the summed intention-empathy score and autism traits was unexpected, given that the ToM account of autism predicts lower scores (Baron-Cohen et al., 1985), a prediction that was supported by previous findings on autism traits and ToM (Atherton & Cross, 2019; Gökçen et al., 2016; Nijhof et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Regarding our secondary analysis, the lack of a significant correlation between the summed intention-empathy score and autism traits was unexpected, given that the ToM account of autism predicts lower scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Baron-Cohen et al., 1985)</ref>, a prediction that was supported by previous findings on autism traits and ToM <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Atherton & Cross, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Gökçen et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Nijhof et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: However, not all previous studies have found ToM difficulties in autism (for a critical review, see Gernsbacher & Yergeau, 2019; Loukusa et al., 2023), and several authors have raised issues with the ToM hypothesis in autism (e.g., Long et al., 2025; Milton, 2012) and the validity of ToM tasks more generally (Long et al., 2025; Quesque & Rossetti, 2020).
text.formatted: However, not all previous studies have found ToM difficulties in autism (for a critical review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Gernsbacher & Yergeau, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Loukusa et al., 2023)</ref>, and several authors have raised issues with the ToM hypothesis in autism (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Long et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Milton, 2012)</ref> and the validity of ToM tasks more generally <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Long et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Quesque & Rossetti, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Note that our Faux Pas Recognition Test was a translation of the German multiple-choice version of the test, which focused on clinical groups other than autism (Burghardt et al., 2025), whereas the original task was open-format (Stone et al., 1998).
text.formatted: Note that our Faux Pas Recognition Test was a translation of the German multiple-choice version of the test, which focused on clinical groups other than autism <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Burghardt et al., 2025)</ref>, whereas the original task was open-format <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Stone et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: These changes may have influenced the task's relevance for autism.

Nevertheless, our findings contribute to the broader discussion about whether such ToM tasks measure important reallife social abilities that are different in autism (Long et al., 2025; Quesque & Rossetti, 2020).
text.formatted: Nevertheless, our findings contribute to the broader discussion about whether such ToM tasks measure important reallife social abilities that are different in autism <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Long et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Quesque & Rossetti, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Another unexpected finding is the positive correlation between autism traits and DR.
Based on the RFT, one would expect a negative correlation, namely that people with more autism traits would perform worse on DR (Kavanagh et al., 2020; Rehfeldt et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Based on the RFT, one would expect a negative correlation, namely that people with more autism traits would perform worse on DR <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Kavanagh et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Rehfeldt et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: In a previous study, we did not observe a significant correlation between DR and the full AQ in a large general adult sample (Nevejans et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In a previous study, we did not observe a significant correlation between DR and the full AQ in a large general adult sample <ref type="bibr">(Nevejans et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Because both this study and Experiment 2 in our previous study included a DR task and AQ, we performed a post-hoc random-effects meta-analysis, combining AQ-Short and DR task scores from both studies (Ntotal = 284; see Appendix C for full analysis and results).
This analysis revealed a significant meta-analytic positive correlation across studies (r = .17, p = .004).

Because this suggests that higher autism scores are associated with better DR performance, our results raise doubts about the proposal that autism is linked to poorer DR performance (e.g., Rehfeldt et al., 2007) and that training DR may serve as a useful intervention strategy (e.g., Belisle et al., 2016; Gilroy et al., 2015; Lovett & Rehfeldt, 2014).
text.formatted: Because this suggests that higher autism scores are associated with better DR performance, our results raise doubts about the proposal that autism is linked to poorer DR performance (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Rehfeldt et al., 2007)</ref> and that training DR may serve as a useful intervention strategy (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Belisle et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Gilroy et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Lovett & Rehfeldt, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: However, generalization of these results to autism is limited, as we assessed autism traits in a general population sample.

Although many participants scored above the AQ-Short cut-off score (28%), which may indicate eligibility for a diagnosis of autism, we cannot generalize these findings to individuals with formal autism diagnoses, especially since the AQ-Short was primarily developed for research purposes and is not a diagnostic instrument.

Although a higher percentage than the actual prevalence rate is to be expected when sensitivity is prioritized, the observed percentage of participants exceeding the cut-off is notably higher than the estimated prevalence of autism in the general population (1%; Zeidan et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Although a higher percentage than the actual prevalence rate is to be expected when sensitivity is prioritized, the observed percentage of participants exceeding the cut-off is notably higher than the estimated prevalence of autism in the general population (1%; <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Zeidan et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In our previous research using Prolific samples, up to 11% of participants also scored above the 50-item AQ cut-off (Nevejans et al., 2026; Experiment 1), suggesting a possible selection bias toward individuals with elevated autism traits on Prolific, at least for this type of research.
text.formatted: In our previous research using Prolific samples, up to 11% of participants also scored above the 50-item AQ cut-off <ref type="bibr">(Nevejans et al., 2026</ref>; Experiment 1), suggesting a possible selection bias toward individuals with elevated autism traits on Prolific, at least for this type of research.

text.text: This warrants further investigation; nevertheless, it resulted in sufficient variation in autism traits for our correlational analyses.

To conclude, we found a relationship between DR and high-level ToM (i.e., the summed intention-empathy score), but only a weak relationship between DR and low-level ToM in a post-hoc analysis, and the latter correlation disappeared when controlling for general cognitive ability.
Although these findings could suggest a relationship between DR and ToM, they are at odds with RFT.

Since RFT positions DR as the functional prerequisite for all perspective-taking, an association with high-level ToM that bypasses low-level ToM challenges the theory's hierarchical prediction that DR directly supports the most basic levels of ToM, whereas high-level ToM might require additional skills (Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004; Kavanagh et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Since RFT positions DR as the functional prerequisite for all perspective-taking, an association with high-level ToM that bypasses low-level ToM challenges the theory's hierarchical prediction that DR directly supports the most basic levels of ToM, whereas high-level ToM might require additional skills <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barnes-Holmes et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Kavanagh et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, it could be that observed correlations between DR and vignette-based high-level ToM tasks depend on shared task characteristics, or other influential factors in the included tasks, rather than a link between DR and ToM abilities.

Future research should test whether the relationship between DR and ToM remains when controlling for the (verbal) format of the tasks, and for other relevant abilities, such as verbal ability or relational responding more generally.
If not, the shared variance might simply reflect other cognitive skills or effort.

Notably, DR showed a small but positive correlation with autism traits across two studies (see Appendix B), indicating that individuals with higher autism trait scores performed better on this task, which is a finding opposite to our expectation and questions whether training DR in autism is a useful intervention strategy.
Typically, RFT predicts that autism traits should be associated with lower performance, not advantages, in the relational framing skills that are supposed to underpin perspective-taking.
Moreover, performance on the Faux Pas Recognition Test did not show any relation to autism traits, which raises questions about its usefulness to autism research on social abilities.
Hence, future research should assess how performance on these tasks relates to real-life social skills and whether they are relevant for the social difficulties reported by individuals with autism.
